clinicalPearls: Entomophthoromycosis is a chronic subcutaneous fungal infection caused by the Entomophthorales, principally Conidiobolus coronatus and Basidiobolus ranarum, seen in tropical Africa, Asia and Latin America
Unlike the angioinvasive mucormycoses of immunocompromised patients, these infections typically occur in immunocompetent hosts and are slow, localised and non-angioinvasive
Conidiobolus infection (rhinofacial/rhinoentomophthoromycosis) affects adults, producing painless, firm swelling of the central face, nose and paranasal tissues that can cause gross disfigurement

Basidiobolus infection presents mainly in children as a firm, mobile, painless subcutaneous swelling of the limbs, shoulder or trunk with a well-defined edge, and can less commonly involve the gastrointestinal tract
Gastrointestinal basidiobolomycosis mimics abdominal malignancy or inflammatory bowel disease and is often diagnosed only after surgery
Diagnosis is histological, showing broad, thin-walled, sparsely septate hyphae surrounded by eosinophilic material (the Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon), with culture for confirmation
Prolonged medical therapy with agents such as oral potassium iodide or azole antifungals is used, sometimes combined with surgery, but rhinofacial disease can leave permanent disfigurement
reference.pathophysiology: The Entomophthorales are environmental saprophytes of soil and decaying vegetation and are also found in the gut of amphibians and reptiles. Infection follows implantation into subcutaneous tissue through minor trauma or insect contact, or, for Conidiobolus, inhalation of spores into the nasal mucosa. The fungi grow slowly within subcutaneous or submucosal tissue, eliciting a chronic granulomatous and eosinophilic inflammatory response rather than invading blood vessels, which distinguishes them clinically from the acute mucormycoses. Progressive local extension produces firm, indurated swelling; gastrointestinal disease arises from mucosal implantation and causes inflammatory masses.
additionalDifferentials: Inflammatory bowel disease or abdominal malignancy (for the gastrointestinal form)
Rhinoscleroma or other causes of destructive facial swelling
additionalInvestigations: Biopsy with histology showing broad sparsely septate hyphae and the Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon
Fungal culture to identify Conidiobolus or Basidiobolus
Full blood count (peripheral eosinophilia is common)
Imaging (CT/MRI) to define the extent of facial or abdominal disease
Endoscopy and biopsy for suspected gastrointestinal involvement
Assessment of immune status to distinguish from mucormycosis
redFlags: Progressive facial swelling threatening the airway, orbit or vision
Gastrointestinal disease with obstruction, perforation or a mass mimicking cancer
Rapid progression or angioinvasive features suggesting mucormycosis instead
Extensive disfiguring disease unresponsive to therapy
reference.prognosis: Subcutaneous basidiobolomycosis of the limbs often responds well to prolonged medical therapy, whereas rhinofacial conidiobolomycosis frequently leaves permanent facial disfigurement despite treatment; gastrointestinal disease carries higher morbidity and can be serious if diagnosed late.
pitfalls: Confusing indolent entomophthoromycosis with aggressive angioinvasive mucormycosis and mismanaging accordingly
Stopping prolonged therapy prematurely, leading to relapse
Missing gastrointestinal basidiobolomycosis, which mimics malignancy or inflammatory bowel disease
Failing to obtain adequate tissue for histology and culture
Underestimating the disfigurement and functional impact of rhinofacial disease
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Prolonged systemic antifungal therapy, most often oral itraconazole or another azole, continued for months until the induration resolves
Potassium iodide as an adjunct or alternative agent, particularly in subcutaneous basidiobolomycosis
Surgical debridement or resection for obstructing gastrointestinal masses and for reconstruction of disfiguring rhinofacial disease, combined with antifungal cover
Monitor peripheral eosinophilia and use serial imaging to track regression of facial or abdominal masses
Reconstructive and plastic surgery for residual rhinofacial disfigurement once infection is controlled
Distinguish from angioinvasive mucormycosis, as its urgency and management differ substantially
Multidisciplinary care involving infectious diseases, surgery and gastroenterology for gastrointestinal disease
